items.stem: Which reagent reduces propanone to propan-2-ol?
items.answer: sodium tetrahydridoborate(III), NaBH₄
items.markingKey: CH₃COCH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.

items.stem: Explain why aldehydes and ketones have lower boiling points than the alcohols from which they are made.
items.answer: Carbonyls have permanent dipole–dipole forces but no O–H, so they cannot hydrogen bond with each other; alcohols do hydrogen bond.
items.markingKey: no hydrogen bonding in carbonyls [1]; alcohols hydrogen bond, stronger forces [1]

items.stem: Explain why an aldehyde is distilled off as it forms during the oxidation of a primary alcohol.
items.answer: The aldehyde is volatile (lower bp than alcohol) and is removed before it can be oxidised further to the carboxylic acid.
items.markingKey: lower boiling point, removed [1]; prevents further oxidation to acid [1]

items.stem: Kenji, a student in Dubai, wants to make 2-methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO, from an alcohol and then reduce a sample back to the alcohol. Name the alcohol and give the reagents and conditions for each step, with equations using [O] and [H].
items.answer: 2-methylpropan-1-ol; warm with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (excess alcohol) and distil off the aldehyde as it forms; (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH + [O] → (CH₃)₂CHCHO + H₂O; NaBH₄; (CH₃)₂CHCHO + 2[H] → (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH
items.markingKey: 2-methylpropan-1-ol [1]; warm with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (excess alcohol) and distil off the aldehyde as it forms [1]; (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH + [O] → (CH₃)₂CHCHO + H₂O [1]; NaBH₄ (aqueous/alcoholic) [1]; (CH₃)₂CHCHO + 2[H] → (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH [1]

items.stem: Sofia, a student in Mumbai, wants to make propanone, CH₃COCH₃, from an alcohol and then reduce a sample back to the alcohol. Name the alcohol and give the reagents and conditions for each step, with equations using [O] and [H].

items.stem: An industrial chemist in Istanbul produces propanal by oxidation of an alcohol. (a) Suggest why its boiling point is lower than that of the alcohol. (b) Give its molecular formula and Mr.
items.answer: (a) No O–H, so no hydrogen bonding between molecules; only dipole–dipole forces. (b) C₃H₆O; 58.0

items.stem: What is the organic product when pentanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO, is reduced with NaBH₄?

items.stem: Explain why NaBH₄ reduces C=O but not C=C bonds.
items.answer: H⁻ is a nucleophile and attacks the δ+ carbon of the polar C=O bond; the non-polar C=C is electron-rich and does not attract nucleophiles.
items.markingKey: C=O polar, δ+ C attacked by H⁻ [1]; C=C non-polar/electron rich [1]

items.stem: What type of mechanism occurs when HCN reacts with ethanal?
items.answer: nucleophilic addition
items.markingKey: CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon.

items.stem: Describe the role of the intermediate in the mechanism of HCN addition to a carbonyl compound.
items.answer: CN⁻ attack produces a negatively charged alkoxide intermediate (O⁻), which accepts H⁺ from HCN (or water) to form the hydroxynitrile, regenerating CN⁻.
items.markingKey: O⁻ intermediate [1]; protonated by HCN, regenerating CN⁻ [1]

items.stem: Explain why the carbonyl carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.
items.answer: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polar and the carbon is δ+, attracting the lone pair of a nucleophile.
items.markingKey: O more electronegative / bond polar [1]; δ+ carbon attracts nucleophile [1]

items.stem: Describe, with the aid of curly-arrow descriptions, the mechanism of the reaction between pentan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, and HCN. Name the product.
items.answer: CN⁻ attacks δ+ C; C=O π bond breaks to give O⁻; O⁻ protonated by HCN; product 2-hydroxy-2-methylpentanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CH₂C(CH₃)(OH)CN.
items.markingKey: curly arrow from C of CN⁻ lone pair to δ+ carbonyl C [1]; C=O π electrons move to O, forming O⁻ intermediate [1]; O⁻ takes H⁺ from HCN (arrow from O⁻ to H), regenerating CN⁻ [1]; 2-hydroxy-2-methylpentanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CH₂C(CH₃)(OH)CN [1]

bubbling HCN gas from a cylinder

items.stem: What is the product when pentanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO, reacts with HCN (from KCN and dilute acid)?

items.stem: Explain why the reaction of HCN with propanone does not give optical isomers.
items.answer: The product, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN, has two identical CH₃ groups on the new carbon, so it has no chiral centre.
items.markingKey: two identical CH₃ groups [1]; no chiral centre so no optical isomers [1]

items.stem: A student in Cape Town claims that in the reaction of HCN with ethanal, H⁺ attacks the carbonyl oxygen first. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: A student in Nairobi claims that the product of HCN and ethanal is optically active because it has a chiral centre. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. The product has a chiral centre, but a racemic mixture forms (equal attack from either side of the planar C=O), so it is not optically active.

items.stem: Which reagent gives an orange precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones?
items.answer: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH)

items.stem: Explain why aldehydes give a positive result with Tollens' reagent but ketones do not.
items.answer: Aldehydes have an H on the carbonyl carbon and are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids, reducing Ag⁺ to Ag; ketones cannot be oxidised without breaking C–C bonds.
items.markingKey: aldehydes oxidised (to acid/carboxylate) [1]; Ag⁺ reduced to Ag; ketones not oxidised [1]

items.stem: Explain why the 2,4-DNPH test alone cannot distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone.
items.answer: Both contain C=O and both form an orange precipitate; a second test (Fehling's or Tollens') is needed.

items.stem: Describe a chemical test to distinguish between butanal and pentan-2-one. Give the observation for each compound.

items.stem: Describe a chemical test to distinguish between propanal and ethanol. Give the observation for each compound.

items.stem: Nadia studies the reaction of carbonyl compounds with HCN in a quality-control laboratory. Explain why the carbonyl carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.
